questions.stem: Keys arrive in sorted order. How do a plain BST and an AVL tree compare for search?
questions.hint: This checks that you can link insertion order to tree height and search cost: a search needs at most one comparison per level.

options.text: Plain BST: a chain with O(n) search. AVL tree: rebalanced after each insertion, so its height and its search stay O(log n)
Both give O(log n) search, because both are binary search trees
options.explanation: A plain BST has no balance guarantee: sorted input makes it a chain.

options.text: Both become chains, because sorted input always produces a chain
options.explanation: The AVL tree rotates as keys arrive, so it never becomes a chain.

questions.stem: A plain BST with 1,000 keys may need 1,000 comparisons for one search. An AVL tree with the same keys needs at most 14. Why?
questions.hint: This checks that you can explain what an AVL tree guarantees: rebalancing keeps the height, and so the search path, short.

options.text: Insertion order can make a plain BST a chain of 1,000 levels; the AVL rule keeps the height at most 13, so a search needs at most 14 comparisons
The AVL tree uses balance factors during the search to skip levels
The plain BST visits every node during a search
options.explanation: Search follows one path in both trees; the plain BST’s path can just be much longer.

questions.stem: Enter the balance factors of 20 and 30, then decide whether this is an AVL tree.
questions.hint: This checks heights and balance factors: height counts edges down to a leaf, and bf = h(right) − h(left), with an empty branch counted as −1.

wrongAnswers.feedback: The sign is reversed. The balance factor is the height of the right branch minus the height of the left branch. Node 20: its right branch is empty (height −1) and its left branch has height 1, so bf = −1 − 1 = −2. A taller left branch gives a negative number.
An empty branch has height −1, not 0. Node 20: its right branch is empty (height −1) and its left branch has height 1, so bf = −1 − 1 = −2.

The sign is reversed. The balance factor is the height of the right branch minus the height of the left branch. Node 30: its right branch has height 0 and its left branch has height 2, so bf = 0 − 2 = −2. A taller left branch gives a negative number.

feedback.correct: Node 20: its right branch is empty (height −1) and its left branch has height 1, so bf = −1 − 1 = −2. Node 30: its right branch has height 0 and its left branch has height 2, so bf = 0 − 2 = −2. This is not an AVL tree: 20, 30 and 60 break the rule.
feedback.incorrect: Node 20: its right branch is empty (height −1) and its left branch has height 1, so bf = −1 − 1 = −2. Node 30: its right branch has height 0 and its left branch has height 2, so bf = 0 − 2 = −2. This is not an AVL tree: 20, 30 and 60 break the rule.

An empty branch has height −1, not 0. Node 50: its right branch has height 1 and its left branch is empty (height −1), so bf = 1 − (−1) = +2.

The sign is reversed. The balance factor is the height of the right branch minus the height of the left branch. Node 60: its right branch has height 0 and its left branch has height 2, so bf = 0 − 2 = −2. A taller left branch gives a negative number.

questions.stem: 25 was just inserted. Find n, name the case and perform the rotation(s).
questions.hint: This checks that you can carry out the rotation(s): the child moves up around its parent, and its inner subtree changes sides.

wrongAnswers.feedback: One rotation about 50 does not fix an inside case: the tree is still unbalanced. Rotate about the child first (left rotation about 20), then about 50.
For an inside case, rotate about n’s child first (this turns it into an outside case), then about n.
Rotate towards the shorter branch: if n’s left branch is too tall, the final rotation about n is a right rotation; if its right branch is too tall, a left rotation.

feedback.correct: Node 50 is n (bf −2): Case 2 (LR). Left rotation about 20, then right rotation about 50. Result: 30(20(10, 25), 50(·, 60)).
feedback.incorrect: Node 50 is n (bf −2): Case 2 (LR). Left rotation about 20, then right rotation about 50. Result: 30(20(10, 25), 50(·, 60)).

feedback.incorrect: Node 30 is n (bf +2): Case 3 (RL). Right rotation about 50, then left rotation about 30. Result: 40(30(10, ·), 50(45, 60)).

questions.stem: Insert 37 into this AVL tree and rebalance. Build the final tree.
questions.hint: This checks the whole insertion: insert as in a BST, update balance factors on the way up, then fix the first unbalanced node with the rotation(s) for its case.

wrongAnswers.feedback: One rotation about 40 does not fix an inside case: the tree is still unbalanced. Rotate about the child first (left rotation about 35), then about 40.
For an inside case, rotate about n’s child first (this turns it into an outside case), then about n.
Rotate towards the shorter branch: if n’s left branch is too tall, the final rotation about n is a right rotation; if its right branch is too tall, a left rotation.
Fix the first unbalanced node on the way up from the new key (40), not the root.
After the fix at 40, the subtree has its old height again, so no node above it needs a rotation.

feedback.correct: Node 40 is n (bf −2): Case 2 (LR). Left rotation about 35, then right rotation about 40. Result: 20(10(5, 15), 30(25, 37(35, 40))).
feedback.incorrect: Node 40 is n (bf −2): Case 2 (LR). Left rotation about 35, then right rotation about 40. Result: 20(10(5, 15), 30(25, 37(35, 40))).

questions.stem: An online exam system stores 30,000 student numbers. Numbers are added at registration in increasing order and looked up thousands of times during an exam. Which structure, and why?
questions.hint: This checks that you can recognise a good fit for an AVL tree: data searched often that must stay in sorted order.

options.text: A plain BST: it is simpler, and BST search is always O(log n)
options.explanation: Increasing numbers make a plain BST a chain, with O(n) search.

options.text: An unsorted list: adding a number is O(1), which matters most here
options.explanation: Lookups happen thousands of times; each would be O(n) in an unsorted list.

options.text: An AVL tree: frequent lookups need guaranteed O(log n) search, and increasing numbers would make a plain BST a chain

questions.stem: What is the strongest reason to use an AVL tree for a spell checker’s word list?
questions.hint: This checks that you can justify the choice from the AVL tree’s properties: guaranteed O(log n) search, at the cost of extra work on updates.

options.text: AVL trees use less memory than other trees
options.explanation: They store a height in every node, so they use slightly more.

options.text: AVL search uses balance factors to find words faster
Words are looked up constantly and may be loaded in alphabetical order; the AVL tree keeps every lookup O(log n)
